lessons.title: Arrays: many values, one name
lessons.goal: Store a row of values and walk through them with a loop.
explain: An array holds a fixed number of values of the same type, one after another in memory. int temps[4] makes four boxes, reached as temps[0] to temps[3].
The size is fixed at compile time and the array does not know its own length in a useful way - you keep the count in a separate constant. The first index is 0, so the last one is size - 1.

example.title: Four days of temperature
example.output:
day 1: 28
day 2: 31
day 3: 30
day 4: 33
hottest 33
bytes 16
notes: SIZE must be a compile-time constant, not a variable that changes
the first box, not the zeroth - counting starts at zero

predict.q: What does temps[4] do when the array has 4 elements?
options: Reads memory past the array - undefined behaviour
Throws an error you can catch
predict.why: Valid indexes are 0..3. There is no bounds check at run time, so index 4 reads whatever follows in memory.

quiz.q: How many elements does int a[5] hold?
quiz.why: The number in the brackets is the count, and valid indexes are 0 to 4.

quiz.q: Why keep the size in a named constant?
options: One place to change, and loops cannot disagree with the array
quiz.why: If the size lives in one constant, changing it updates the declaration and every loop together.

quiz.q: What is the last valid index of an array with n elements?
quiz.why: Starting at 0 shifts everything down by one, so n elements end at n-1.

activity.goal: Given five step counts, print the total and the average using a loop.
hints: Start an int total = 0; before the loop and add each element inside.
Loop with for (int i = 0; i < DAYS; ++i).
The average is total / DAYS - both ints, so it stays whole.

lessons.mistake: Looping to i <= SIZE, which reads one element past the end. The comparison is always < SIZE.
lessons.recap: An array is a fixed row of values indexed from 0 to size-1.

lessons.title: Vectors: the array that grows
lessons.goal: Use std::vector when you do not know the size in advance.
explain: std::vector is an array that knows its length and can grow. push_back adds to the end, pop_back removes the last, size() tells you how many there are.
The range-for loop for (int s : scores) visits every element without any index arithmetic - use it when you do not need the position.

example.title: A growing list of scores
notes: an empty vector that grows as needed
adds one element at the end

predict.q: What does scores[10] do on a vector with 3 elements?
predict.why: operator[] does not check. .at() does check and throws std::out_of_range, which is why it is the safer choice while learning.

quiz.q: Which adds 7 to the end of v?
quiz.why: push_back appends. v[7] writes at an index that does not exist yet - a serious bug.

quiz.q: What is the difference between size() and capacity()?
options: size is how many you have, capacity is how many fit before it grows
capacity is the number of bytes
quiz.why: Vectors over-allocate so push_back is usually cheap; capacity reports that reserved room.

quiz.q: When is a fixed array a better choice than a vector?
options: When the count is known at compile time and never changes
quiz.why: A fixed array has no bookkeeping and no allocation, which matters in small embedded code.

activity.goal: Read numbers until the user types -1, store them in a vector, then print the count and the biggest.
hints: The read itself can be the loop condition: while (std::cin >> n && n != -1)
push_back each n that survives the condition.
Track the biggest as you go with if (n > biggest) biggest = n;

lessons.mistake: Using a range-for loop while adding or removing elements. The range is captured once, so the loop can read memory that has moved.
lessons.recap: vector grows, knows its size, and pairs with range-for.

lessons.title: References: another name for the same box
lessons.goal: Change the caller's variable from inside a function.
explain: A reference is an alias. int& score means 'score is another name for the caller's variable', so writing to it writes to the original.
Without the &, the parameter is a copy and the caller never sees the change. Use const & when you only want to read a big object without copying it.

example.title: By value versus by reference
notes: a reference - no copy is made
its score is a separate box that dies when the function ends

predict.q: Why does the second call change nothing?
options: Because the parameter is a copy of ana, not ana itself
Because void functions cannot change anything
predict.why: The copy is modified and then destroyed when the function returns; the original is untouched.

quiz.q: What does int& mean in a parameter list?
options: A reference: the caller's variable, not a copy
A pointer that can be null
quiz.why: A reference must be bound to an existing object and cannot be null, unlike a pointer.

quiz.q: Why use const std::string& as a parameter?
options: To prevent the function reading it
To avoid copying a long string while still forbidding changes
quiz.why: const & is the standard way to pass something big cheaply and safely.

quiz.q: Can a reference be re-bound to a different variable later?
options: No - it is bound for its whole life
quiz.why: Assignment through a reference changes the value it refers to, never which object it refers to.

activity.goal: Write void double_it(int& n) that doubles the caller's number, and use it on 21.
hints: The parameter must be int& with the ampersand, or the caller sees nothing.
Inside: n = n * 2;
Call it once, print, call again, print.

lessons.mistake: Returning a reference to a local variable. The local dies at the end of the function and the reference points at nothing.
lessons.recap: & binds a second name to the same object; const & reads without copying.

lessons.title: Pointers: the address of a value
lessons.goal: Read a pointer, follow it, and know what nullptr means.
explain: A pointer stores an address. int* p = &battery; puts the address of battery into p, and *p reads the value at that address.
The same * means two things: in a declaration it marks the type as 'pointer to int'; in an expression it dereferences. nullptr means 'points at nothing' and is the correct empty value.

example.title: Following an address
example.output:
value 87
through pointer 87
after write 50
is null 1
notes: dereference: go to the address and read what is there
writing through the pointer writes to battery
the empty pointer - always check before dereferencing

predict.q: What happens if you dereference a nullptr?
predict.why: There is no object at that address. On Windows this is an access violation, which ends the program immediately.

quiz.q: What does &x give you?
quiz.why: & is the address-of operator. In a declaration it also makes a reference - context decides which meaning.

quiz.q: Which is the safest empty pointer?
quiz.why: nullptr has its own type and cannot be confused with an integer, so overloads resolve correctly.

quiz.q: Why are pointers considered risky for beginners?
options: An invalid pointer still compiles and crashes later, or silently corrupts memory
quiz.why: Nothing checks that a pointer is valid. That is why modern C++ prefers references and smart pointers.

activity.goal: Write void boost(int* p) that adds 10 through the pointer, and call it on a score of 30.
hints: The function takes int* and changes *p inside.
Pass the address: boost(&score);
Inside: *p += 10;

lessons.mistake: Confusing & in a declaration (int& r - a reference) with & in an expression (&x - the address). Same symbol, different job.
lessons.recap: A pointer holds an address; * follows it and & takes it.

lessons.title: Structs: grouping facts together
lessons.goal: Bundle related values into one type of your own.
explain: A struct is your own type made of named parts. Once a Robot has a name, a battery and an awake flag, you can pass one Robot around instead of three separate variables.
Structs are usually written in a header so every file can use them. Members are public by default, which is the main difference from a class.

example.title: Two robots
example.output:
Five Sides battery 87 awake
Spare battery 12 asleep
Five Sides battery 57 awake
notes: a new type - note the semicolon after the closing brace
members are filled in the order they are declared
pass by reference so nothing is copied

predict.q: What does five.battery -= 30 do to the Robot in main?
options: Nothing, because report took a const reference
It changes five, because five is the object itself
predict.why: The change happens in main on the real object, before report is ever called. The const& only protects r inside report.

quiz.q: What is the difference between a struct and a class in C++?
options: Struct members are public by default; class members are private by default
Classes can hold functions, structs cannot
quiz.why: That is the only language-level difference. Both can have methods, constructors and inheritance.

quiz.q: Why prefer a vector<Robot> over three parallel arrays?
options: The pieces of one robot stay together and nothing can drift out of step
quiz.why: Parallel arrays break the moment you sort one of them - the name and its score stop matching.

quiz.q: What does the semicolon after a struct's closing brace do?
options: It ends the type definition - required
quiz.why: A struct definition is a statement and needs its semicolon. Forgetting it produces confusing errors.

activity.goal: Add a level member (int) to Robot, fill in two robots, and print "name level battery" for each.
hints: Aggregate initialisation follows member order: name, level, battery.
Robot a{"Five Sides", 3, 87};
Print with a.name << " " << a.level << " " << a.battery << "\n".

lessons.mistake: Declaring a struct with the same name as a variable, or forgetting that aggregate initialisers are positional - add a member in the middle and every initialiser shifts.
lessons.recap: A struct is a named bundle of values you can copy, pass and store.

lessons.title: Classes: data plus behaviour
lessons.goal: Attach functions to your type and guarantee it starts in a valid state.
explain: A class is a struct that also owns its behaviour. The constructor runs when the object is created, so an object can never exist half-built.

Member functions that do not change the object are marked const, which lets them be called on const objects and documents your intent. The trailing _ on member names is a common convention to tell them apart from parameters.

example.title: A counter that cannot be uninitialised
notes: the constructor - same name as the class, no return type
initialiser list: members are built directly, in declaration order
const promises this function does not change the object

predict.q: What is printed if you delete count_(0) from the initialiser list?
options: The count starts at an unpredictable value
predict.why: An int member is left uninitialised by default. The class would compile and then print junk.

quiz.q: When does a constructor run?
options: Only when you call it by name
quiz.why: Construction is automatic at the point of creation - that is the whole point of a constructor.

quiz.q: What does the const at the end of a method signature mean?
options: The method does not modify the object
The method cannot be called twice
quiz.why: It makes this const, so the compiler enforces that no member is changed inside.

quiz.q: Why mark a single-argument constructor explicit?
options: It stops the compiler silently converting a value into your type
quiz.why: Without explicit, a function taking Counter could be called with a string and the conversion would happen invisibly.

activity.goal: Write a class Battery with charge_ (int) starting at 100, a use(int) method that subtracts but never goes below 0, and level() const.
hints: charge_ already starts at 100, so the constructor body can stay empty - or use an initialiser list.
Clamp with if (charge_ - amount < 0) charge_ = 0; else charge_ -= amount;
Print b.level() after each use.

lessons.mistake: Assigning members inside the constructor body when an initialiser list would do - members are built first anyway, so the body assignment is a second write.
lessons.recap: A class keeps data private and guarantees a valid state through its constructor.

lessons.title: Encapsulation: protecting the rules
lessons.goal: Keep an object's rules true by refusing bad changes.
explain: Encapsulation means the outside world asks your object to do things instead of reaching into its data. The object can then refuse anything that would break its own rules.
A rule that must always hold is called an invariant. Here the invariant is 'the balance is never negative', and withdraw() is the only way to change it.

example.title: A wallet that cannot go negative
notes: returns whether it worked, so callers can react
both rules checked before touching the data
nothing outside the class can write balance_ directly

predict.q: Why does the second withdraw print denied?
options: Because 100 is not a valid number
Because it is more than the remaining balance of 50
Because withdraw can only be called once
predict.why: The guard rejects any amount larger than the current balance, so nothing is subtracted.

quiz.q: What is an invariant?
options: A rule that must always be true for the object
quiz.why: Invariants are the promises the class keeps; every public method must preserve them.

quiz.q: Why return bool from withdraw instead of silently ignoring a bad amount?
options: The caller can tell the difference between success and refusal
quiz.why: Silent failure hides bugs. A return value lets the caller show a message or retry.

quiz.q: What breaks encapsulation?
options: A getter that returns a copy
A public member the caller can write freely
quiz.why: A public writable member lets anyone break the invariant without the class noticing.

activity.goal: Add a transfer(Wallet& other, int amount) method that moves money between wallets and refuses if the source is short.
hints: A transfer is withdraw from this, then deposit into other - reuse the existing methods.
Return false immediately if withdraw fails, before depositing.
bool transfer(Wallet& other, int amount) { if (!withdraw(amount)) return false; other.deposit(amount); return true; }

lessons.mistake: Adding a setBalance() 'just in case'. It hands the invariant back to the caller and every guarantee you built disappears.
lessons.recap: Private data plus checked methods keeps an object's rules true.

lessons.title: map and set: looking things up
lessons.goal: Store values by key and keep a collection of unique items.
explain: std::map<Key, Value> keeps pairs sorted by key and finds them quickly. m[key] creates the entry if it is missing, which is convenient but can hide typos - count() or find() tell you whether a key really exists.
std::set holds unique values in sorted order and drops duplicates automatically. Both are usually implemented as balanced trees, so lookups are logarithmic rather than a scan.

example.title: Scores by name
example.output:
Ana 90
count 2
has Robot 0
Ana=90 Ben=95 
set size 3
1 2 3
notes: creates on first use, then updates

predict.q: What does scores["Robot"] do if Robot was never added?
options: Creates Robot with value 0 and returns it
predict.why: operator[] default-constructs the missing value. Use .at() to throw instead, or .count() to check first.

quiz.q: Which is safe when the key might not exist?
quiz.why: at() throws std::out_of_range and find() returns end() - both tell you the truth. operator[] invents an entry.

quiz.q: What does a set remove automatically?
quiz.why: Sets store each value at most once; inserting an existing value is a no-op.

quiz.q: When would an unordered_map be a better choice?
options: When you only need fast lookup and do not care about order
quiz.why: Hash maps give average constant-time lookup but no ordering - pick based on whether you iterate in order.

activity.goal: Count how many times each word appears in a sentence using a map, then print each word and its count.
hints: The loop is while (stream >> word), which reads one word at a time.
++counts[word] both creates the entry and increments it.
A map iterates in sorted key order, so no extra sorting is needed.

lessons.mistake: Reading with m[key] inside a loop over the same map - it can insert a new element and invalidate the iteration you are in.
lessons.recap: map is key to value, set is unique values, and both keep order.

lessons.title: The algorithm library
lessons.goal: Replace hand-written loops with tested standard algorithms.
explain: The standard library already contains the loops you keep writing: sort, find, count_if, max_element, accumulate. They are tested, optimised, and say what they mean.
Most take a pair of iterators (begin and end) and some take a predicate - a function returning bool that decides what counts.

example.title: Five scores, four questions
notes: sorts in place, ascending by default
the 0 is the starting value - use 0.0 for a decimal sum
a lambda: a small function written where it is used

predict.q: What does std::find return when the value is missing?
predict.why: Algorithms work on iterator ranges, so 'not found' is signalled by returning end(). Compare against it before dereferencing.

quiz.q: Why prefer std::sort over a hand-written bubble sort?
options: It is faster, correct, and already tested
quiz.why: The standard sort is a hybrid algorithm with good worst-case behaviour; a hand-rolled sort is usually both slower and wrong on edge cases.

quiz.q: What is a predicate?
options: A function returning bool used to decide something
quiz.why: count_if, find_if and sort all accept one to decide membership or order.

quiz.q: What does accumulate need as its third argument?
quiz.why: It starts from that value and adds each element - which also sets the result type.

activity.goal: Sort the scores descending, print them, then print how many are below 70.
hints: Descending is a third argument: std::sort(b.begin(), b.end(), std::greater<int>{});
Include <functional> for std::greater.
count_if with a lambda returning s < 70.

lessons.mistake: Calling an algorithm on a range that is being modified, or forgetting that sort changes the order of the original vector.
lessons.recap: Reach for <algorithm> before writing a loop by hand.

lessons.title: Reading and writing files
lessons.goal: Save data between runs and read it back.
explain: std::ofstream writes, std::ifstream reads, and closing happens automatically when the object goes out of scope. The stream is your handle to the file.
Always test whether the file opened. while (in >> name >> score) is the standard read loop: it stops when the data runs out or the file is malformed.

example.title: Write two lines, read them back
notes: the braces close the file as soon as the block ends
the stream converts to bool: false means the open failed
reads until the data runs out

predict.q: Why does the write happen inside its own { } block?
options: So the file is closed before anything tries to read it
Because ofstream must be in a block
predict.why: Buffered data is flushed when the stream is destroyed. Closing first guarantees the reader sees the complete file.

quiz.q: Which class writes to a file?
quiz.why: o stands for output. ifstream reads, and fstream can do both.

quiz.q: What does while (in >> a >> b) do at end of file?
options: Stops, because the read fails and the condition is false
quiz.why: A failed read makes the stream false, which ends the loop - no explicit check needed.

quiz.q: Why check if (!in) right after opening?
options: A missing or locked file otherwise silently reads nothing
quiz.why: Without the check you get an empty result and no explanation - the classic 'my data vanished' bug.

activity.goal: Write three high scores to a file, read them back, and print the best one.
hints: Open the writer in its own { } block so it closes before reading.
Read with while (in >> name >> score) and keep bestName/bestScore.
Compare with > and update both name and score together when a better one appears.

lessons.mistake: Writing and reading the same file in one scope without closing the writer first - the reader can see an empty or half-written file.
lessons.recap: ofstream writes, ifstream reads, and the read loop ends itself.

lessons.title: Declarations, definitions, and many files
lessons.goal: Understand what goes in a header and why programs are split up.
explain: The compiler reads one file at a time. A declaration tells it the shape of something (name, parameters, return type) so it can compile a call; the definition supplies the body, and the linker joins them later.
A header (.hpp) holds declarations and is included by everyone. A source file (.cpp) holds definitions. Include guards or #pragma once stop a header being included twice.

example.title: The same idea in one file
notes: a declaration: ends with a semicolon, no body
the definition: same signature, with a body
main only compiles because the declarations come first

predict.q: What happens if you delete both declaration lines but keep the definitions below main?
options: main fails to compile - the compiler has not seen the names yet
predict.why: The compiler works top to bottom. Calls above the first sight of a name are errors, not linker errors.

quiz.q: What belongs in a header?
quiz.why: Headers are copied into every file that includes them, so they hold declarations. Bodies in a header cause duplicate-symbol errors at link time.

quiz.q: What does #pragma once do?
options: Stops the same header being included twice in one translation unit
quiz.why: It is a widely supported include guard. The portable alternative is #ifndef/#define/#endif.

quiz.q: Which error appears when a function is declared but never defined?
quiz.why: The call compiles fine because the declaration exists; the linker is the one that cannot find the body.

activity.goal: Add a declaration for average(int, int) above main, and define it below main so the program prints 7.5.
hints: A declaration is the signature with a semicolon: double average(int a, int b);
The definition repeats the signature and adds a body returning (a + b) / 2.0.
Replace the placeholder line with the real call once the declaration exists.The 2.0 matters - int division would print 7.

lessons.mistake: Putting a function body in a header that several files include - the linker then sees the same definition many times.
lessons.recap: Declare in headers, define in source files, and let the linker join them.

lessons.title: Project: robot fleet board
lessons.goal: Combine structs, vectors and algorithms into a small report generator.
explain: This project keeps a fleet of robots, sorts them by battery, flags the low ones and counts how many are ready. It is the shape of a real status screen.
Notice that the sorting and counting rules are written once, as small lambdas, instead of being spread through the printing loop.

example.title: fleet.cpp
example.output:
Five Sides 87
Red-Bot 45
Spare 12 LOW charging
Blue-Bot 8 LOW charging
ready 4
notes: the comparator: true means a comes before b

predict.q: If Five Sides dropped to 10 and stopped charging, what would the last line say?
predict.why: It would no longer be >= 20 and it is not charging, so it drops out of the count: three remain.

quiz.q: Why sort before printing?
options: The report reads best highest-first, and it shows the sort in action
quiz.why: There is no technical need - it is a presentation choice, and exactly the kind of thing a status board does.

quiz.q: What would happen if the comparator returned a.battery >= b.battery?
options: Undefined behaviour - a strict weak ordering is required
quiz.why: A comparator must be a strict ordering: comp(a,a) must be false. Using >= breaks that and can crash the sort.

quiz.q: How would you print only the robots that are ready?
options: Add another loop with the same if
Use std::copy_if or filter inside the loop
quiz.why: Filtering belongs in the iteration step, either with an if inside the loop or an algorithm that selects.

activity.goal: Add a charge(int amount) step before the report: every charging robot gains the amount (max 100), then print the new total battery across the fleet.
hints: Only charging robots gain: if (r.charging) r.battery += 20;
Clamp with std::min(100, r.battery + 20).
Sum with std::accumulate over a lambda: [](int sum, const Robot& r) { return sum + r.battery; }

lessons.mistake: Forgetting the & in for (Robot& r : fleet), which copies each robot and throws the changes away.
lessons.recap: Struct plus vector plus algorithm is enough for a real report.
